content: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the esophagus caused by an antigen-mediated immune response. It is characterized by clinical symptoms of esophageal dysfunction and histological findings of at least 15 eosinophils per high-powered field under a microscope. Current diagnostic guidelines for EoE no longer require a lack of response to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) but still recommend ruling out other causes of esophageal eosinophilia. The primary goals of EoE treatment include alleviating clinical symptoms, resolving esophageal eosinophilia and other histological abnormalities, improving endoscopic findings, enhancing esophageal function and quality of life, minimizing treatment-related adverse effects, and preventing disease progression and complications. There is currently no cure for EoE, necessitating long-term management. Standard treatment approaches include dietary modifications, esophageal dilation, and pharmacologic therapies such as corticosteroids, biologics, and PPIs. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of medical treatments for EoE. The review included 41 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 3,253 participants. Eleven studies focused on pediatric patients, while the remainder included both children and adults. Four studies involved patients with inactive disease, while the rest included those with active disease. The review examined 19 different treatment comparisons, with a focus on corticosteroids and biologics compared to placebo. Fourteen studies compared corticosteroids to placebo for inducing remission. Corticosteroids were associated with a modest improvement in clinical symptoms when measured dichotomously (20% higher improvement, risk ratio [RR] 1.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08 to 2.80, low certainty) and continuously (standard mean difference [SMD] 0.51, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.85, low certainty). Corticosteroids led to a significant improvement in histological outcomes, with a 63% higher rate of histological improvement when measured dichotomously (RR 11.94, 95% CI 6.56 to 21.75, high certainty) and a notable improvement when measured continuously (SMD 1.42, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.82, low certainty). Endoscopic improvement with corticosteroids was less clear, with little to no improvement observed when measured dichotomously (RR 2.60, 95% CI 0.82 to 8.19, low certainty) but some improvement when measured continuously (SMD 1.33, 95% CI 0.59 to 2.08, low certainty). Corticosteroids were associated with slightly fewer withdrawals due to adverse events compared to placebo (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.96, low certainty). Nine studies compared biologics to placebo for inducing remission. Biologics showed little to no difference in clinical symptom improvement when measured dichotomously (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.52, low certainty) but demonstrated better clinical improvement when measured continuously (SMD 0.50, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.78, moderate certainty). Biologics resulted in a significant improvement in histological outcomes, with a 55% higher rate of histological improvement when measured dichotomously (RR 6.73, 95% CI 2.58 to 17.52, moderate certainty). However, the evidence for histological improvement when measured continuously was uncertain (SMD 1.01, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.66, very low certainty). Biologics showed little to no difference in endoscopic improvement when measured dichotomously (low certainty), and the evidence for continuous measures of endoscopic improvement was inconclusive (SMD 2.79, 95% CI 0.36 to 5.22, very low certainty). Withdrawals due to adverse events occurred at similar rates between biologics and placebo (RR 1.55, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.74, low certainty). In conclusion, corticosteroids may improve clinical symptoms and lead to significant histological improvement compared to placebo, though their effect on endoscopic improvement is less certain. They may also result in fewer withdrawals due to adverse events. Biologics may not improve clinical symptoms when measured dichotomously but may show improvement when measured continuously. They lead to significant histological improvement when measured dichotomously, though the evidence for continuous measures is uncertain. Biologics may not improve endoscopic outcomes, and their safety profile appears comparable to placebo.
